html:
A long square in Rome that keeps the shape of the Stadium of Domitian, begun about 80 AD, where Romans watched games, the agones; the name Navona grew from the old name, Circus Agonalis. After the fall of the western empire the stadium fell into ruin and was quarried for stone. Only a few pieces of it remain, but the oval of its track survives as the open space of the square.

It became a public square in the last years of the 15th century, when the city market moved here from the Capitoline. Its present look comes from Pope Innocent X, pope from 1644 to 1655, whose family palace, the Palazzo Pamphili, faces the square. In the middle stands the Fountain of the Four Rivers by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, finished in 1651 and topped by an ancient obelisk brought in pieces from the Circus of Maxentius. Facing it is the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone, built by Francesco Borromini, the Rainaldis and others; the palace gallery was designed by Borromini and painted by Pietro da Cortona.

Two older fountains by Giacomo della Porta stand at the ends: the Fountain of the Moor at the south, from 1575, to which Bernini added the Moor wrestling a dolphin in 1673, and the Fountain of Neptune at the north, from 1574, whose Neptune was added only in 1878. From 1652 to 1866 the square was flooded on weekends in August for festivals of the Pamphili family. The market moved to the Campo de' Fiori in 1869.
